title: Laying on hands (Luke 4:31–44)
hook: at sunset they bring the sick, and he lays his hands on every one

segments.voice: Yesterday, the edge of the cliff in Nazareth, and a man who walked through the crowd. Your line was he went his way. When praise turned this week, did you keep walking? Day five hundred eighteen.

Capernaum, a city of Galilee. The day began on the sabbath, with Jesus teaching in the synagogue. Now the sun is going down, and the streets start to fill. Luke doesn't say why the crowd waits for sunset; some readers connect it with the sabbath, which ends at sundown. Mats, stretchers, people leaning on cousins' shoulders, children being carried. Everyone with someone sick is heading to the same door, the house of a man named Simon.
screen: `WAITING FOR THE SUN TO GO DOWN.`

segments.voice: The day began in the synagogue, where a man possessed by an unclean spirit cried out, and Jesus said: "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." People were stunned: "What a word is this!" Then he went to Simon's house, where Simon's mother-in-law lay "taken with a great fever." Luke, whom tradition remembers as a physician, says Jesus "stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them." She gets up and serves the table. Then sunset, and the verse that gives today its name: "Now when the sun was setting, all they that had any sick with divers diseases brought them unto him; and he laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them." Every one of them. Not a wave from the doorway to the whole crowd. Not a blessing in bulk. One by one, hands on each person. Laying on hands was an old gesture in Israel's scriptures, for blessing and for setting someone apart. Christians kept it. Today hands are laid on people in ordination, in confirmation in some churches, and in prayer for the sick, from Catholic and Orthodox anointing to Pentecostal healing services. And here's the ending: at dawn, Jesus slips away to a deserted place. The crowds find him and beg him to stay. He says: "I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also: for therefore am I sent." Full attention to each person at night. And in the morning, he moves on, because, he says, that is what he was sent for.
screen: `THE FEVER LEFT; SHE ROSE AND SERVED.`
then, large: `HE LAID HIS HANDS ON EVERY ONE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay attention to one person fully. Settle, and breathe. Picture that doorway at sunset, the line of people, and one pair of hands, one person at a time. Now bring to mind the people you'll see today. Who usually gets the half of you that's looking at a screen? A child, a partner, a parent on the phone, a coworker, the person at the register. Choose one. Picture giving them all of you for five minutes: eyes up, phone away, listening to the end of their sentences. Let that picture be clear before the bell. If you pray, you can hold that person before God now. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Capernaum. The city where, at sunset, Jesus laid his hands on every sick person brought to Simon's door, one by one.

Your line: every one of them. Today, give one person your whole attention. And look back at the week: a boy in the temple, a crowd at the river, a desert, a hometown, a doorway at sunset. Day five hundred eighteen, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Churches lay hands on people in ordination, some in confirmation, and in prayer for the sick, including the Catholic and Orthodox anointing of the sick and healing prayer in Pentecostal and charismatic churches.

original.note: Greek: a laying on. the noun in Acts 8:18 and Hebrews 6:2; Luke 4:40 uses the verb.

trapdoor: what you thought: laying on hands is a church ritual.
what it means: in Luke, it's personal: Jesus touches each sick person one by one, all evening.
what a scholar hears: the gesture was already old in Israel's scriptures, for blessing and setting apart, and churches kept it for ordination, confirmation and healing.

notes: Sunset as the end of the sabbath, after which carrying the sick was allowed, is a common explanation; Luke does not say it outright. Confirm framing.
Luke as a physician rests on Colossians 4:14 and tradition; phrased 'often remembered as'.
Descriptions of the laying on of hands across churches (ordination, confirmation, anointing of the sick, Pentecostal healing prayer) are general. Confirm.
Week-end look-back placed in the carry.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook rewritten: it stated as fact that people waited all afternoon because carrying was forbidden until the sabbath ended at sundown, which Luke does not say; now 'some readers connect it with the sabbath'. Also 'a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee' to Luke's 'a city of Galilee', and 'a fisherman named Simon' to 'a man named Simon' (his fishing is tomorrow's story, Luke 5); cut 'would have taken hours' and the empty close 'both are part of the same love'; 'many churches' to 'some'; original note made accurate (Luke 4:40 uses the verb).
